A lot of cooking and eating. In Gardena, we are eating and living together. The thread of our thriving that was always there has grown.
Meals are prepared and eaten with ease around large tables. Chefs have acute measurements so that all that is made is eaten or repurposed.
Food is plant based and we are selective of what we grow based on conditions.
All the beings that have existed return and new combinations are created too. Food is made and distributed and is no longer a commodity -that was never a decent idea.

The kinder-elder centers have gardens where native food, herbs, and flowers are grown by elders, little ones, and middlings with intention and attention to the seasons and pollinators. Harvesting is a joyful celebration and day-to-day cooking and eating are communal activities.

Food is not put in a grocery store and purchased to go bad in a refrigerator. It is grown in gardens- large and small and used per day or per meal. The stewards of the land are teachers and show us how to grow all the food we need. How to raise the animals, how to harvest the wheat for bread, how to prepare the meals. Maybe families have breakfast and lunch in their homes and the whole town comes together to eat dinner and share their own harvest.
We eat spicy mango jam and crunchy chocolate covered seed pods made from our own community gardens.
We have accessible learning for all including in how to grow and have good food. Food knowledge and ways.
We have become resilient and strong. Food is medicine. Breath is filled with life.

Kids read poems before they eat breakfast. People cook with poetry in their recipes. Food comes from each other for each other with each other. Food bursts with flavors in our mouths and we are giddy. We are diabetes free!
We've found ways to cultivate food and farm. We live harmoniously with water as it rises and recedes.
Simplicity. Food as nourishment. Food as medicine. Growing beans. Saving seeds.

Now, we understand ourselves as wild and deeply connected to and situated among all other wild species. In this way we've learned how to feed ourselves and dwell more porously and we are connected to the wild. Now, it would never occur to build a fence or a wall to stop widespread movement of any wild thing. A child laughs at the idea as silly- as if trying to stop the wind or a rising tide.
The resources, production and preparation of food are tended to with care and honor.
My asparagus patch is still being used by my neighborhood.
There are plots of communally stewarded land in each neighborhood - for gardens. Donated to the commons - starting small. Middle class, homeowners, and slowly the rich people followed.

Food is harvested bioregionally, through collective wildland tending. And people identified with their ecosystem and all its interrelated parts. The salmon nation, the wild rice nation, the acorn nation, the pinion nation.

Beef isn’t very healthy for us and cattle aren’t very healthy for our environment. How would our earth look like without cattle- what would be the negative and positive impacts. Would affect farmers, restaurants, land ownership, jobs, slaughterhouses, butchers, farm community populations. Would affect use of land where cattle graze.

In the face of scarcity, we turned our individual contributions to generating what was needed for the winter months of food storage. We held our commitment to our whole and our connections with other communities to share without abandon until all within our city and our neighbors were sustained.
It is a community effort/enjoyment to plant, cultivate, harvest, process, cook and eat food together.

Food and sustenance for the tribes will reflect a time long before the destructive waves of capitalism - healthy foods that the new soil can grow. Meals are communal, those who prepare food are as revered as any other in the tribe. There is no person young or old who will know hunger - in fact there is no word in any language in the new places being cultivated that describes hunger.
People have food and it’s plentiful and colorful.
Our relationship with food animals has shifted. We see animals with dignity and empathy–and how it’s tied to our own humanity.
We’ve re-taken our relationship with land – food. People live multigenerationally. Know how to farm, raise food. Understand where food comes from. The lives it comes from.
Free food, because gardens exist.

Content: Community gardens thriving. Rivers revived. Caring for interdependence at each and every step

There are food hubs in every community. There are always things like fresh apples and carrots, shared freely. The community makes sure all nourishment needs are met at these hubs – with rotating foods depending on abundance and season. Kids and adults are always rotating in and out for what they need and what they share.
There are rest and digest chairs that have a heartbeat, rocking, and hugs. These chairs are near the food hubs.

Community kitchens and cafes serve the community and are stocked largely by highly successful regenerative agricultural operations that steward the land in community with one another. We know this way of being is sacred, and that we are fortunate to have remembered how to center it in all action.

All of our food comes from within 50 miles of where we live. Small community farms are built right in the middle of cities. Occasionally we can get food from afar but we are not dependent on anything being shipped or flown to us. People have hydroponic gardens at home. We have no need for plastics - everything we use comes from the earth and goes back to the earth.

All goods are edible or plantable into the earth to return nourishment and nutrients to our soil systems - there is no plastic. There is a universal understanding of how to love and nurture a fellow human, creature, plant, or thing to grow and flourish - this means that children are educated in spaces where they can both learn essential lessons and play as their full selves; it means that they come home to families that are supportive and loving places to land and foster curiosity and safety. Food production has transformed to be an activity that all learn about and participate in - everyone has a connection to the food they eat. Communities barter and trade to ensure bounty.

People know the people who grew or made almost all of the food that sustains them and their families. The food is seasonal and sustainable, with a variety of vegetables, fruits, legumes, and grains providing the bulk of the calories.

A restaurant has young people and elders filming a multi-generational food competition, where elder/youth pairs from all different cultures are preparing the dishes they will enter. The food tastes like it is supposed to taste.
Actually educating our children about how food grows, capturing and storing energy, managing our own (literal) shit – returning it to the soil.
Food forests create food, shelter, medicine without it having to be a cleared and tightly managed farm.  It is also an important place for learning and school.

Food forests aren’t cleared lands but food bearing plants integrated within the natural landscape. There are small, individual dwellings within the food forests. 10-18 people per dwelling in pods is what is typical – in parenting and elder pods. There’s a main pod and then others with aunties and uncles. Children can live in their main dwelling but also go from time to time to other dwellings for a time.

If you are here and alive, you eat.  Everyone has healthy food to eat.  Whole groups of people explore recipes families have passed down – get good ingredients.  Food is made seasonally and locally – usually within 50 miles.  We have a meal brigade that brings good food to people who can’t get there – or central places for people to come to.  This is some people’s role and other people rotate through.
There is no suffering required for me to feed my body. We are eating things that are not birthed or born from suffering.

There is a local garden or several every few blocks that residents can go and grab their own fruits, vegetables, herbs and more and care for the land collectively. No one takes more than what they need. The garden thrives seasonally and features animals and plants local to the area.
People get to try all the delicious foods from everywhere

In fact, communal eating is everywhere. Around imu, people learn and tell the stories of their food — the intentional eating feeds the body, the spirit, and the relationships that make up community. It also connects us to the encouragement of our ancestors. Every bite, an affirmation of the work that got us here and that we carry on. Every bite, appreciation for both the delicacies of the land and the deliberate choices made so we can taste them.

That communal eating is just one of many experiences that embody another core aspect of our thriving future. It is nutritious. Not just in food, but absolutely in food. The air is sweet and nutrient filled, absent the chemicals and carcinogens that characterized other eras. Fish are free of chemicals and plastics, and soil is alive and thriving. Fueled by these nutrient rich foods (grown in nutrient rich environments) and this nutrient rich air, families regularly visit natural places to hike and be together, and through these relationships both people and nature are healthy.
